scenario: A 24-year-old man has a wide irregular tachycardia at 180 and a history of delta waves. Pressure is 120/70 and he is awake. A classmate gives intravenous metoprolol.
question: Which drug is safe, and why is metoprolol dangerous?
options: Adenosine as a diagnostic drug in a wide irregular rhythm
explanation:
Atrial fibrillation with a preexcitation pattern is not treated with an AV-nodal blocker. Procainamide or cardioversion is used. Nodal blockers can speed conduction down the accessory path. Blocking the node sends more impulses down the extra path and can cause ventricular fibrillation. Procainamide or cardioversion is the plan. Loscalzo J, Fauci AS, Kasper DL, Hauser SL, Longo DL, Jameson JL, eds. Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st ed. McGraw Hill; 2022.

Procainamide or electricity. Not metoprolol
Intravenous metoprolol — A nodal blocker is the danger.
Adenosine as a diagnostic drug in a wide irregular rhythm — Adenosine is not used for an irregular wide rhythm.
Digoxin to slow the node — Digoxin is also unsafe in preexcited fibrillation.
Observation of a rate of 180 — The rhythm needs a drug that acts on the extra path, or electricity.
citation: Loscalzo J, Fauci AS, Kasper DL, Hauser SL, Longo DL, Jameson JL, eds. Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine. 21st ed. McGraw Hill; 2022.
